newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Samsung looks to non-memory chips to rescue profits.
newsitem.headline: Samsung looks to non-memory chips to rescue profits.

text.p: Samsung Group's announced $8 billion investment in non-memory chips is designed to shield its battered profits from wild swings in the price of memory chips, industry analysts said on Thursday.
But while analysts generally hailed the announcement, they cautioned that entry to the non-memory market would be a hard slog over many years.
On Wednesday Samsung announced it would spend seven trillion won ($8.1 billion) over the next five years to achieve $15 billion turnover in non-memory chips by 2005.
By that year, the sector would account for 50 percent of total Samsung semiconductor sales, up from 20 percent now, the company said in a statement.
"It is certainly the direction Samsung needs to be looking in," said Matt Cleary, an electronics analyst at HG Asia.
"Samsung's experience in 1996 has been a blunt lesson in the volatile nature of the memory market. By developing a strong non-memory portfolio Samsung could ease the volatility of memory profits."
Profits of group flagship Samsung Electronics crashed to 164.2 billion won in 1996 from 2.5 trillion in 1995 due to a plunge in global prices for dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips.
Last year the unit price of 16-megabit DRAM chips, most widely used in personal computers, fell 80 percent.
Unlike memory chips that store data, non-memory chips perform much more complicated tasks. They range from application-specific integrated circuits to digital signal processors and microprocessors.
The Samsung statement said by 2005 the company hoped to have five percent of the global market in non-memory chips against its current two percent.
But analysts warned it would take time for Samsung to become a major player in the non-memory field.
"It's very difficult to buy your way into non-memory business. A lot of times niche areas have already been dominated and it's hard for the newcomer," said Cleary.
"It will take five years for Samsung to build non-memory chip designing skills and establish good client relationships," said Jon Chong-hwa, an electronics analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities.
Samsung group chairman Lee Kun-hee told electronic division heads in Tokyo the company would develop its own technology in non-memory chips.
"Growth in non-memory chip business is vital to secure profits and add value to our semiconductor business," the statement quoted him as saying.
"It's quite a natural move," said Jon.

"Samsung has neglected non-memory chips because DRAMs have been very profitable before a slump last year. It now feels the need to diversify its revenue and strengthen presence in semiconductor field through investment in non-memory chips."

Samsung said it would spend four trillion won by 2005 in chemical, environmental and bio-engineering fields and on developing thin-film transistor liquid crystal displays, code division multiple access stations and lithium batteries.
The group was seeking three trillion won profit on 19 trillion won turnover in 2005 from investment in those areas. But analysts said this could be risky.
"Samsung is already diversified enough. It should concentrate on what it's good at and focus on that," said Cleary.
